title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps

epigraph.quote: Price is what you pay; value is what you get. Whether we're talking about socks or stocks, I like buying quality merchandise when it is marked down.
epigraph.author: Warren Buffett, 2008 Shareholder Letter

web_blocks.title: 7.1 Deconstructing the $231.04 Share Price & Historical Valuation Bands

web_blocks.html: As of the November 24, 2026 close, Lowe's (NYSE: LOW) trades at $231.04 per share [31]. That price values 561.0M diluted shares at a $129.63B market cap and a $167.91B enterprise value, reflecting $37.55B in debt and $3.74B in cash [2, 31]. Shares sit 21.16% below their 52-week high ($293.06) and 29.47% above their 52-week low ($178.45) [31]. On TTM metrics, LOW trades at 19.37x P/E ($11.93 TTM EPS), 18.17x forward P/E, 16.22x P/FCF (6.17% yield), and 13.09x EV/EBITDA [31]. The stock also pays a 2.12% dividend yield ($4.90 TTM; 40.08% payout ratio) [31].

Historical trading bands show why shares have moved sideways. Over the past decade (2016–2026), Lowe's averaged 19.44x trailing P/E (range 13.66x–33.18x), 16.65x P/FCF, and 1.20x P/S [25, 26, 27]. Today's 19.37x trailing P/E and 16.22x P/FCF sit right on those 10-year medians [25, 26, 31]. Yet the stock fell 8.55% over the past five years prior to dividends [31]. Investors are weighing $7.65B of annual free cash flow against three years of falling retail traffic and $10.1B of debt-funded Pro M&A [1, 2]. That debt load paused Lowe's signature share-buyback engine until mid-2027 [28].

web_blocks.takeaway: Lowe's is not priced for perfection like high-multiple defensive staples; at 18.17x forward P/E and a 6.17% FCF yield, the market is pricing in muted low-single-digit organic growth and execution skepticism on FBM/ADG integration.

web_blocks.title: 7.2 Reverse DCF: What Growth & Margin Is Baked Into $231.04?

web_blocks.html: Institutional underwriting starts with a Reverse DCF: what growth rate does $231.04 already assume? Audited FY2025 FCF was $7,651M, and 9M FY2026 FCF reached $7,026M ($8,690M CFO minus $1,664M capex) [1, 2]. On $7,650M of normalized annual FCF, a $129.63B market cap implies a 5.90% starting FCF yield (6.17% on Finviz TTM) [31]. Using the verified November 24, 2026 4.92% 10-year Treasury yield (from our market ledger) plus 0.75 beta × 6.0% equity risk premium gives a 9.42% cost of equity. At 9.42% cost of equity and 3.0% terminal growth, $231.04 implies roughly 3.8% annual FCF growth over ten years.

That 3.8% implied hurdle is modest, yet higher rates tighten the valuation band and demand explicit sensitivity math. At a 9.42% cost of equity, a 4.5% 10-year FCF CAGR values LOW at $244.91/sh ($137.4B equity), which would leave sub-1.0:1 asymmetry from $223.49. Reaching our $268.00 Base Target on DCF requires 5.5%–6.0% annual FCF growth ($264.09–$274.24/sh at 9.42% CoE; or 5.0% FCF growth at 9.05% CoE using a 5.5% ERP). That 5.5%–6.0% path is achievable without a housing boom: 3% organic sales growth, $120M–$180M in annual interest savings as $4B+ of debt is retired, and FBM/ADG cross-sell synergies. Once leverage hits 2.75x in mid-2027, redirecting $4B–$5B/yr of surplus FCF into buybacks retires 3.0%–3.8% of shares annually on top of the 2.12% dividend [28].

web_blocks.the_number: 12–18 Month Base Intrinsic Value: $268.00/sh (+16.0% vs. $231.04 CMP; +19.9% vs. $223.49 support high)

Two-year bridge to $13.65 (+$1.74): +$0.85 from 2.5%–3.0% organic comps and FBM/ADG synergies, +$0.22 from $150M lower net interest, +$0.35 from H2 FY2027 share buybacks, and +$0.32 from diesel/PPI margin normalization. web_blocks.title: 7.3 Quantitative Peer Benchmarking: Home Improvement & Building Supply

web_blocks.html: Peer benchmarking highlights Lowe's valuation discount relative to capital efficiency. Home Depot (HD) trades at 22.60x forward P/E and 23.36x P/FCF versus LOW at 18.17x and 16.22x [31]. Yet Finviz ROIC is virtually identical: 20.77% for HD versus 21.03% for LOW [31]. HD earns a premium for its ~50% Pro mix and 119 bps wider TTM operating margin (12.35% vs. 11.16%). Still, a 20% forward P/E discount already prices in Lowe's smaller Pro scale and temporary leverage. Other peers look far pricier on cash flow: BLDR trades at 22.70x forward P/E with 2.13% operating margin, FND trades at 25.67x with 5.56% ROIC, and TSCO trades at 70.48x P/FCF [31].

web_blocks.caption: Lowe's (LOW) vs. Listed Home Improvement & Building Supply Peers (Verified Close: November 24, 2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: LOW offers the highest FCF yield (6.17% / 16.22x P/FCF) and lowest forward P/E (18.17x) among profitable large-cap home improvement compounders, paired with 21.03% ROIC that matches Home Depot (20.77%).

web_blocks.title: December 9, 2026 Analyst Conference: The Near-Term Valuation Catalyst
paragraphs: On November 18, 2026, CEO Marvin Ellison deferred FY2027 guidance to the December 9, 2026 Analyst Conference [30]. Analysts trimmed price targets toward $240–$250 (Finviz consensus: $248.84) after FY2026 adjusted margin guidance slipped to ~11.5% on $6/gallon diesel costs [29, 30, 31].

December 9 is the key near-term valuation test. Credible FBM/ADG synergies and a firm 11.5%+ FY2027 margin floor can re-rate LOW toward 19.5x–20x. Any margin slip below 11.5% would likely pull shares back to the $200–$215 base.

book_paragraphs: Now that you and I have spent six chapters studying Lowe's business without peeking at a stock quote, we can finally open the market screen and ask the question that separates great businesses from great investments: what is Wall Street asking us to pay for every dollar of Lowe's earnings and cash flow? As of the November 24, 2026 close, Lowe's trades at $231.04 per share — a $129.6 billion equity value and a $167.9 billion enterprise value once you add back the $37.55 billion debt stack left behind by the Foundation Building Materials and Artisan Design Group acquisitions.

Here is the first thing that jumps off the page when you compare today's price to history. Over the past decade, investors paid an average of 19.44 times trailing earnings and 16.65 times free cash flow to own Lowe's. Today, at 19.37 times trailing earnings, 18.17 times forward earnings, and 16.22 times free cash flow — a 6.17 percent cash flow yield — Lowe's is sitting right on its ten-year valuation average, and at a steep four-and-a-half-turn forward earnings discount to its bigger twin, Home Depot, which trades at 22.60 times forward earnings and 23.36 times free cash flow.

Why is the market refusing to pay a Home Depot multiple for a business that generates over 21 percent return on invested capital? You already know the answer from our forensic audit in Chapters 5 and 6. Wall Street hates two things in retail: falling store traffic and paused buybacks. Lowe's just posted its sixth consecutive quarter of positive comparable sales (+1.8 percent in Q3 FY2026), yet customer transactions fell 1.7 percent, gross margin dropped 124 basis points on $6-per-gallon diesel and wholesale mix, and management cut full-year adjusted operating margin guidance to 11.5 percent. On top of that, the $10.1 billion Pro acquisition spree pushed lease-adjusted leverage to roughly 3.0 times EBITDAR, forcing CFO Brandon Sink to freeze share repurchases until mid-2027.

Let us run a Reverse DCF together to see how pessimistic that pricing really is. Starting from $7.65 billion of normalized annual free cash flow and applying an 9.42 percent cost of equity (using the 4.92 percent 10-year Treasury yield) with a 3 percent terminal growth rate, a $231 share price only requires Lowe's to compound free cash flow at roughly 3.8 percent per year over the next decade. Think about how modest that hurdle is. Lowe's does not need another 2020 pandemic renovation mania to justify $231. It only needs inflation-level comparable sales growth, steady 11.5 to 12.0 percent adjusted operating margins, and the mechanical math of capital allocation once debt paydown finishes in mid-2027.

Walk through that cash-flow bridge with me. Lowe's produces $7.6 billion to $8.2 billion of free cash flow every year and spends roughly $2.75 billion on its Dividend King payout (currently yielding 2.12 percent). That leaves roughly $5 billion of surplus cash every twelve months. Through mid-2027, that $5 billion pays down debt — eliminating $120 million to $180 million of annual interest expense and transferring enterprise value directly from bondholders to equity holders. Starting in the second half of fiscal 2027, that same $5 billion can repurchase roughly 3.5 percent of the company's shares every year. Add 3 percent organic operating profit growth, 3 percent share retirement, and a 2.1 percent dividend, and you get an 8 to 10 percent baseline return before any housing-cycle recovery.

Look across the peer table and the value gap becomes even sharper. Builders FirstSource trades at 22.7 times forward earnings while posting negative 8.25 percent revenue growth and a 2.1 percent operating margin. Floor & Decor trades at 25.7 times forward earnings with 5.6 percent ROIC. Tractor Supply trades at 19.2 times forward earnings and 70 times free cash flow. Only Lowe's combines a 6.17 percent free cash flow yield, 21 percent ROIC, and an 18.2 times forward multiple. That is why our normalized 12-to-18-month base-case intrinsic value lands at $268 per share — roughly 19.6 times $13.65 of normalized FY2027–FY2028 earnings, still a 13 percent multiple discount to Home Depot.

Yet we must stay ruthlessly honest about the near-term risk. On December 9, 2026, Marvin Ellison and Brandon Sink will host Lowe's Analyst and Investor Conference to lay out fiscal 2027 guidance. Wall Street's average price target sits around $249, and the stock has already rallied 16.56 percent over the past month ahead of that event. Valuation says Lowe's is attractively priced for patient capital, not dirt cheap enough to ignore a stretched chart or an unconfirmed margin floor. To decide when and where we actually want to bid, we need to read the tape in Chapter 8.

Let us also test our valuation against the single most common skeptical question: what if Lowe's never deserves Home Depot's multiple, and what if the FBM and ADG acquisitions permanently lower corporate operating margins by 50 to 80 basis points? Even under that conservative framework, notice how forgiving the math at $231.04 — and especially at $211 to $223 — remains. If adjusted operating margins merely stabilize around 11.5 percent on $95 billion to $98 billion of fiscal 2027 and 2028 revenue, Lowe's still generates roughly $10.9 billion to $11.3 billion of operating profit, $7.5 billion to $8.0 billion of free cash flow, and $13.50 to $13.80 of normalized earnings per share once interest expense drops and share repurchases resume. Capitalizing $13.65 of normalized earnings at 19.6 times — right in line with Lowe's own ten-year average of 19.44 times and still three full turns cheaper than Home Depot — delivers our $268.00 base-case fair value without needing a single turn of heroic multiple expansion.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Why a 6.17% Free Cash Flow Yield Matters When Buybacks Pause
book_callouts.text: Investors often treat a temporary share-buyback pause as permanent capital destruction. In reality, when a 21%-ROIC retailer diverts $5 billion of annual surplus cash from buybacks to paying down 5%-coupon acquisition debt, equity holders still capture 100% of that cash flow — first through lower interest expense and reduced financial risk, and twelve months later through a resumed buyback engine.
